note_title: Spoken in Galilee, remembered at the tomb.
note_body: The hard word Jesus gave in Galilee is the very word the angel recalls at the empty grave: remember how He told you. What sounded like defeat was resurrection reading its own itinerary.
lens_gloss: to hand over, to deliver up — the word for betrayal that Scripture also uses for God giving His own Son

note_body: The God who kept Israel's clothes and sandals whole through forty wilderness years is the same Lord who sends His workers out without a second coat. Provision has always traveled with obedience, not with baggage.
lens_gloss: a field-hand, a laborer — Jesus sends His people out as workers whose Father, not their luggage, guarantees the evening meal.

note_body: Matthew heard the same charge Mark records: the truth of who Jesus is was not withheld, only entrusted to God's timing. Restraint was part of the revelation, not a denial of it.
lens_gloss: to charge sternly, command with weight — the same firm word Jesus uses to still storms; holy restraint carries real authority.

note_title: Promised on earth, kept in glory.
note_body: On a dusty road Jesus promised to confess His confessors before the angels of God; in Revelation the risen Lord says it again from the throne. The promise survived the cross and gained a crown.
lens_gloss: to say the same thing, to agree aloud — confession is letting your public voice match what your heart knows of Jesus.

note_title: Grace keeps the old law kindly.
note_body: Moses commanded that a worker's hire be paid before sundown; the lord of the vineyard pays at evening, right on Torah time. Grace never cheats anybody — it just starts the line at the back.
lens_gloss: wages, hire — in this vineyard the pay is measured by the owner's generosity, never by a worker's comparison.

note_title: The Red Sea and the boat.
note_body: Israel stood at the water fresh from wonders and remembered not the multitude of God's mercies; the disciples sat in a boat with the Bread of Life and worried about loaves. Worry is almost always a memory problem.
lens_gloss: to harden into a callus, to petrify — worry left unanswered by remembered mercy slowly calluses the heart's memory.

note_title: A thousand hills, one borrowed colt.
note_body: The God who owns every beast of the forest stoops to say He has need of a tied-up colt. He does not seize what is ours — He dignifies it by asking.
lens_gloss: need, necessity — the Lord who lacks nothing makes gracious room for your offering; His 'need' is your invitation.

note_body: From a pagan hilltop Balaam glimpsed a Star out of Jacob — 'I shall see him, but not now.' On the Bible's last page Jesus claims that Star as His own name, and the far-off promise comes near enough to answer the dark.
lens_gloss: star — a light set against the dark; the Star Balaam saw from a distance now speaks its own name up close.

note_body: Jesus withholds the hour so the heart will stay awake; Luke records His remedy — watch and pray always, that you may stand before the Son of man. Readiness is not scanning the sky; it is keeping company.
lens_gloss: to stay awake, keep alert — watchfulness is love keeping its lamp trimmed, not fear refusing to sleep.

note_title: The beggar the neighbors never saw.
note_body: In Jerusalem the neighbors argued over whether the healed man was even the same beggar — they had passed him for years without truly seeing him. Outside Jericho, Jesus stops for the man the crowd steps around.
lens_gloss: road, way — Bartimaeus sat beside the way until mercy called him; by the chapter's end he follows Jesus in it.

note_body: Mark adds one detail to the same journey: on the far side of Jordan, 'as he was wont, he taught them again.' Jesus carries His faithfulness into every transition — and teaches us to pack ours too.
lens_gloss: to finish, bring to completion — the Lord who finishes His sayings finishes His work; His transitions are completions, never abandonments.

note_body: Jesus pronounces woe on the one through whom stumbling comes; Paul turns that woe into a household habit — judge your own path clean rather than your brother. Love sweeps the road ahead of other people's feet.
lens_gloss: the trip-stick of a snare, a stumbling block — Jesus takes whatever trips His little ones with deadly seriousness.

note_body: The sufferer of Psalm 22 vowed, 'I will declare thy name unto my brethren'; in a crowded house Jesus looks around the circle and says, 'Behold my brethren.' The old promise now has eyes to meet.
lens_gloss: brother, one from the same womb — Jesus stretches the family word until obedient love sits comfortably inside it.

note_body: Matthew hears the cross as the cost of belonging to Jesus; Luke hears the schedule — deny yourself and take it up daily. The cross is not a single dramatic hour but tomorrow's ordinary surrender, offered again.
lens_gloss: the cross, an execution stake — Jesus names the instrument of dying as the daily shape of following Him.

note_body: David sang that God would revive him while he was still in the midst of trouble; Peter promises the God of all grace will personally restore, confirm, strengthen, settle. Both testaments agree — the mending is His work, not yours.
lens_gloss: to mend, as fishermen mend torn nets — the God of all grace repairs what suffering tore and refits it for use.

note_body: Jesus warns His household they will be labeled as their Master was; Peter coaches that same slandered household — live so honestly that the accusers end up glorifying God. The insult is borrowed, and so is the vindication.
lens_gloss: enough, sufficient — becoming like the Teacher is not discipleship's consolation prize; it is the whole reward.

note_body: Peter lays the account before Jesus — we have left all. Paul, further down the same road, runs the numbers again and writes gain in the loss column: everything surrendered for Christ turns out to be profit.
lens_gloss: to release, let go — the Gospels' own word for forgiving; following Jesus begins with an opened hand.

note_title: The water held because Christ did.
note_body: Peter's steps on the sea were never powered by Peter; they answered a single word from Jesus. Paul learned the same physics on dry land — all things, but only through Christ who strengthens.
lens_gloss: the one-word command 'Come' (from erchomai) — Jesus does not lecture Peter across the waves; He simply calls him near.

note_title: Believed and known, kept for life.
note_body: Young Peter pairs the words in the synagogue — we believe and are sure; old John, writing years later, pairs them again — we have known and believed. A true confession does not fade; it settles in and keeps house.
lens_gloss: to know by experience, by living alongside — Peter's certainty grew from shared bread and storms, not from argument.

note_title: What His eyes were fixed on.
note_body: Jesus names Jerusalem, betrayal, and death without slowing His stride; Hebrews tells us why — for the joy set before Him He endured the cross. He could see past the hill, and He invites us to trust the same horizon.
lens_gloss: to hand over, deliver up — a word holding both man's treachery and the Father's giving; Jesus is handed over, yet still leads.

note_body: Matthew keeps the millstone saying almost word for word, because the church needed to hear it twice. The people easiest to overlook are the ones heaven watches closest — handle them as precious, for they are.
lens_gloss: small, little — heaven's word for the easily overlooked; in Jesus' arithmetic the smallest are the most closely guarded.

note_body: Jesus promises some will see the kingdom before tasting death; Hebrews unveils the deeper mercy — He tasted death for every man. Glory can come before the grave only because the grave met Him first.
lens_gloss: to taste, to experience fully — the bitterness Jesus drank down whole so His followers could glimpse the kingdom first.

note_body: When Ahaz was told to ask a sign, the Lord promised one anyway — a virgin's Son, God with us. Generations later men demand a sign from Jesus, never seeing that Isaiah's promised Sign was the very One they questioned.
lens_gloss: a sign, a token pointing beyond itself — they demanded proof on order while the Sign of all signs stood answering them.

note_body: God warned Jeremiah that even his brothers, his father's house, would deal treacherously with him; Jesus walks that same ache through His own hometown. The Son does not pity the prophets from a distance — He joined them.
lens_gloss: without honor, priced low — Jesus knows the ache of being undervalued by those who watched Him grow, and obeys anyway.

note_title: A full net is not the finish.
note_body: The dragnet gathers everything, but the shore does the telling; Luke's question presses the same point — what profit is a whole world's catch if the soul itself is cast away? Mercy gathers wide, and truth still sorts.
lens_gloss: good, sound, worth keeping — the fisherman's word for a catch that proves genuine when the net finally reaches shore.

note_body: In the Song, the bride hears her beloved knocking at night — open to me, my love — and hesitates too long. The risen Jesus takes up the same posture at the heart's door, supper ready, still asking to be let in.
lens_gloss: to knock — present tense, a continuing knock; Jesus will not force the door He died to open, so He keeps knocking.

note_body: Jesus commands watchfulness because the hour is unknown; Paul gives the reason it need not be anxious — salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. Watching is hope sitting up straight, not fear pacing the floor.
lens_gloss: Lord, the One with rightful claim — you are not scanning for an event but keeping house for Someone you belong to.

note_body: Mark shows Jesus pressing the disciples into the boat; John shows what was rising on the shore — a crowd ready to force a crown. Sometimes His firm sending is protection from a danger we never even saw.
lens_gloss: to compel, press firmly — Jesus' leading can be insistent exactly when His reasons are hidden; the pressure was mercy.

note_title: Seek Him while He is near.
note_body: Isaiah pleads for seeking while the LORD may be found; the parable shows the grief of afterward, when the door has closed. Grace holds the door open today — readiness is simply answering while it stands wide.
lens_gloss: afterward, later — the parable's saddest adverb; what love invites today cannot always be borrowed afterward.

note_body: A thousand years before that temple-court question, David's song had already seated the Messiah at God's right hand. Jesus simply lifts the psalm His hearers loved and lets it show them a Lord bigger than their answer.
lens_gloss: master and rightful owner — David calls his own descendant his sovereign, and Jesus lets the title say what the crowd would not.

note_body: Jesus tells the Sadducees that resurrection life is not the old arrangements resumed, and Paul explains why: what goes into the ground corruptible comes up incorruptible. The life ahead is not this one extended — it is this one transformed.
lens_gloss: to stand up again — resurrection is not the old life resumed but life raised to stand in a wholly new order.

note_body: "Thus did Moses... so did he" and "the disciples went, and did as Jesus commanded" are the same plain music. God has always built His holy story out of ordinary people simply doing the thing He said.
lens_gloss: to do, to carry out — obedience in this Gospel is not a feeling about Jesus but a thing actually done.

note_body: Luke names the principle and Matthew shows the welcome: whoever is faithful in the least is trusted with much, and the trusting comes wrapped in the master's own joy. The few things were never small to the Lord watching how they were held.
lens_gloss: joy, gladness — the master's own delight, opened like a room the faithful servant is welcomed to enter.

note_body: Jeremiah watched prophets run whom God never sent, and Jesus warns the same traffic will run in His own name. The test has not changed: not how fast a voice runs, but who sent it.
lens_gloss: to lead astray, to set wandering — deception rarely shoves; it walks a soul off the path one agreeable step at a time.

note_body: Matthew shows Jesus finishing His parables and moving on; Mark tells us why He could — He spoke the word "as they were able to hear it." The Teacher completes His lesson and trusts the seed, never forcing more than a heart can carry.
lens_gloss: to finish, bring to completion — Jesus ends His teaching whole, nothing dropped, then trusts the word to keep working.

note_body: Israel swore Jonathan's rescue with a hair-of-his-head oath, and Jesus reaches for the same measure to describe the Father's care. What a whole army promised one prince, God quietly keeps for every child He counts.
lens_gloss: to count one by one — the Father's knowledge of you is itemized, not approximate; nothing about you is a rounding error.

note_body: Mark's warning says eternal, and Hebrews answers with the same word turned toward hope — eternal redemption, obtained by Christ's own blood. The soul that trembles at the warning is the very soul the Spirit is drawing through the open door.
lens_gloss: to slander, speak against with settled contempt — a hardened verdict on the Spirit's witness, not the anxious stumble of a tender conscience.

note_body: The proverb watched it long before the Pharisees did: a righteous heart studies its answer while a wicked mouth simply pours. Jesus is not policing vocabulary — He is tending the well the words are drawn from.
lens_gloss: the heart — the inner wellspring of thought, desire, and will; the hidden source your spoken words keep quoting.

note_body: Ezekiel was carried in the Spirit into a valley of dry bones; John stood in the Spirit on a prison island. In both places the verdict is the same — exile can change the address, but it cannot silence the Voice.
lens_gloss: breath, wind, Spirit — the air John breathed on Patmos; exile changed his circumstances but never his atmosphere.

note_title: Fame with the Lord inside it.
note_body: Joshua's fame spread because the LORD was with him, and now a greater Joshua's fame reaches even Herod's palace. But hearing about Jesus is not the same as bowing — a rumor received is not a Lord received.
lens_gloss: hearing, report, rumor — what reaches the ear about Jesus; Herod caught the report but never received the Man.

note_title: The prophet saw the thorns first.
note_body: Long before the parable, Jeremiah pleaded: break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Jesus is working the same field — the word deserves soil that has been cleared, not a corner of whatever is already growing.
lens_gloss: thorn — the crowding weed nobody plants on purpose; cares and riches take the field simply by being left to grow.

note_title: Daniel saw this Son of man.
note_body: When Jesus says the Son of man will send forth His angels, He is standing inside Daniel's night vision — the one brought before the Ancient of days and given a kingdom. Holiness matters this much because the King is this real.
lens_gloss: the trip-stick of a snare, a stumbling block — whatever trips others into sin, the King will clear from His field.

note_title: The stones were already spoken for.
note_body: Daniel had seen it centuries out: after Messiah is cut off, the city and sanctuary fall. Jesus is not guessing about the stones — He is reading the prophecy He came to fulfill, and inviting our trust to move from buildings to Him.
lens_gloss: to loosen down, dismantle stone from stone — what looks immovable can be unfastened; only what God holds together holds.

note_body: Israel promised that the man who felled Goliath would make his father's house free. In Jesus the promise comes true the deep way — the Son's victory sets the whole household free, so the children serve from belonging, not to buy it.
lens_gloss: free — the liberty of family members, not the exemption of strangers; the children are free because the house is their Father's.

note_title: First book and last book agree.
note_body: Moses said do not add or diminish; Revelation closes the canon with the same charge. From Sinai's plains to Patmos, God's word asks for hands that receive it whole, not hands that edit it.
lens_gloss: to take away, subtract a portion — trimming God's word costs the trimmer, never the word.

note_body: When fowls came down on the covenant sacrifice, Abram stood there and drove them off. That is the picture for a wayside heart — the word God gives you is worth guarding on the spot, before the devourer arrives.
lens_gloss: to eat down, devour completely — an unreceived word is not merely missed; left on the surface, it gets consumed.

note_title: Hide the word; keep the word.
note_body: Wisdom's counsel is to receive the words and hide them within — treasure buried too deep for a thief. What Jesus mourns in the wayside hearer, the proverb prevents: a word hidden in the heart cannot be snatched off the surface.
lens_gloss: to seize suddenly, snatch by force — the enemy moves fast on a word left lying unguarded on the surface of the heart.

note_body: The Zacharias Jesus names had preached one question — why do you transgress the LORD's commandments? — and was stoned for it in the temple court. Correction refused hardens into violence; correction received becomes the doorway Jesus is holding open.
lens_gloss: blood — spilled life that keeps a voice; God hears every syllable of what violence tried to silence.

note_title: Every secret thing, every idle word.
note_body: The Preacher said God will bring every work and every secret into judgment; Jesus carries the audit down to the idle word. This is not meant to frighten the tongue into silence but to invite it into cleansing.
lens_gloss: idle, literally without work — a word doing no good work; Jesus audits even our throwaway speech so grace can form it.

note_title: The question rose out of prayer.
note_body: Luke lets us see what Mark's roadside hides: Jesus had been alone praying before He asked who men say He is. The question beneath all questions comes to us the way it came to them — from a Savior already talking to the Father about us.
lens_gloss: to put a searching question — Jesus teaches by asking, drawing confession up from the heart instead of pressing it down from outside.

note_body: Isaiah confessed words of falsehood conceived and uttered from the heart — the same pipeline Jesus uncovers beneath the Pharisees' religion. Managed appearances cannot help a heart that needs a Redeemer.
lens_gloss: to make common, render unclean — defilement is not caught from the outside; it leaks from within, where only grace can reach.

note_body: Isaiah says the word of our God stands forever, and Jesus calmly says the same of His own words. That is not a teacher's boast — it is the Son placing His sentences where only God's belong.
lens_gloss: to pass by and be gone — skies and history will exit the stage; His sentences will not.

note_body: The disciples "then understood" about John the Baptist, and on resurrection evening Jesus "opened their understanding" of all the Scriptures. Clarity in His school is not extracted by effort alone — it is given, usually a little further down the road.
lens_gloss: to bring together, connect the pieces — understanding as things finally fitting, a gift that arrives while walking with Him.

note_title: A swept house still needs its Lord.
note_body: In the psalm God longs to fill His people — open thy mouth wide — but Israel would none of Him. That is the ache behind the swept and garnished house: cleaned, arranged, and still unoccupied by the only Guest who makes it safe.
lens_gloss: to arrange, put in order, adorn — a tidied life can still be an unoccupied one; order is not Presence.

note_body: Asaph sang, "I will open my mouth in a parable," and Matthew says Jesus' storytelling fulfilled that very line. The parables were never a new trick — they are an old promise keeping its appointment.
lens_gloss: something laid alongside — a story set next to life so truth can slip past defenses and wake a listening heart.

note_body: Matthew and Mark both kept this small embarrassing scene: disciples tallying loaves while the Bread of Life sits in their boat. The church saved the story because scarcity still talks over Jesus, and He still asks, "Do ye not remember?"
lens_gloss: to reason back and forth within — anxious inner arithmetic that loops loud enough to drown out the Word in the boat.

note_title: A name better than sons and daughters.
note_body: To outsiders who feared they had no place, Isaiah promised a place and an everlasting name within God's walls. Revelation shows the promise kept — the overcomer made a pillar, written all over with the Name that settles whose he is.
lens_gloss: pillar — a load-bearing column set in place for good; he shall go no more out, permanence given, not earned.

note_body: Matthew sets the scene and Mark preserves the sermon: beware of robes and greetings worn for the marketplace. Jesus loves His listeners too much to let performance pass for faithfulness.
lens_gloss: a learner, an apprentice — one who stays close enough for hard teaching to shape the private life, not just the public one

note_body: What the LORD promised a stammering Moses at the bush, Jesus promises His disciples before hostile councils: go, and the words will be given. The mouth is yours; the supply is His.
lens_gloss: to worry ahead of time, to rehearse in anxiety — the advance dread Jesus lifts from His people's shoulders

note_title: Willing and obedient, prophet and parable.
note_body: Isaiah names the two things the vineyard tests: willingness and obedience. The son's yes only mattered when his feet carried it out the door.
lens_gloss: child — the father's summons to work begins with family tenderness, not the cold voice of an employer

note_title: Two wrestlers who would not let go.
note_body: Jacob at the Jabbok and this mother at Jesus' feet hold on the same way: I will not let You go without a blessing. Heaven does not call that rudeness — heaven calls it faith.
lens_gloss: to run toward a cry for aid — her plea is barely a breath long, and it asks Jesus to come running

note_title: Flattery that accidentally told the truth.
note_body: Malachi sketched the faithful messenger — truth in his mouth, walking in peace and equity — and even Jesus' enemies end up reading that portrait aloud. Their trap opens with an accidental confession.
lens_gloss: true, genuine — real all the way through, with nothing staged for the audience or adjusted for approval

note_title: A widow's cry, a servant's debt.
note_body: The prophet's widow did not manage her debt quietly; she cried it out to Elisha, and heaven answered with oil. What we admit, mercy can meet — what we hide keeps the creditor at the door.
lens_gloss: to pay back in full — the very thing the servant cannot do, which is exactly where mercy begins

note_body: Matthew and Luke both keep this answer because the logic holds everywhere: what is divided against itself falls. Jesus casts out darkness with an undivided hand, and He invites the heart to match Him.
lens_gloss: to be split into parts, torn against itself — the inner fracture no kingdom, and no heart, can survive

note_body: The man who asked for a word before stepping onto water is the same one who later confessed, to whom shall we go — Thou hast the words of eternal life. Bold steps are safe only when they start in Jesus' voice.
lens_gloss: to command, to give the word — Peter will not step onto the sea without an order from Jesus' own mouth

note_body: David sang that even an encamped army could not take his confidence, and Jesus turns that song into a command: be not troubled. Steadiness is not denial — it is knowing who holds the end.
lens_gloss: to be alarmed, inwardly shaken by clamor and rumor — the panic Jesus tells His people not to host

note_title: Daniel's night vision finds its throne.
note_body: The One like the Son of man whom Daniel watched approach the Ancient of days is the very King Matthew seats upon the throne of glory. What the prophet saw in the night, the Gospel promises in broad daylight.
lens_gloss: weight, radiance, majesty made visible — the splendor in which the Servant who washed feet finally sits down

note_body: Zechariah heard God say they will look on Me whom they pierced; Revelation answers, every eye shall see Him, even those who did it. The wounds are not erased in glory — they are His identification.
lens_gloss: to pierce through — the wound the world gave Him becomes the mark by which every eye will know Him

note_title: The Psalter saw the sorting coming.
note_body: Psalm 1 already drew the line — the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment — and Jesus confirms that angels will one day trace it. Truth this serious is not meant to terrify the trusting heart but to clarify today's choices.
lens_gloss: to mark off by a boundary, to separate — the final sorting Jesus names plainly and without flinching

note_title: Astonishment that stopped short of faith.
note_body: Matthew records the same homecoming: they were astonished at His wisdom, yet astonishment curdled into offense. Familiarity had memorized Jesus without ever surrendering to Him.
lens_gloss: one's homeland, native place — the familiar ground where wonder must fight hardest to stay alive

note_body: The disciples ask why the teaching comes veiled, and in John Jesus sets a date: the time cometh when I shall shew you plainly. Mystery in His hands is never a locked door — it is a scheduled unveiling.
lens_gloss: a placing alongside — a story laid next to life so hidden things can come near to those who keep asking

note_title: Paul's answer to the Son's warning.
note_body: Jesus warns against being ashamed of Him, and Paul stands up with the reply of a settled heart: I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ. Grace does not make disciples timid — it makes them unashamed.
lens_gloss: to feel shame over, to quietly distance oneself from — the soft denial Jesus says He takes personally

note_title: A mountain, a boat, one Teacher.
note_body: Matthew sets Him on a mountainside; Mark seats Him in a borrowed boat. Jesus makes a pulpit out of whatever is near, which means the place you are sitting right now will do.
lens_gloss: to teach — the patient shaping of hearts that Jesus carries into boats, shorelines, and ordinary rooms

note_body: The disciples ask who ranks highest, and Philippians hands the church its cure: in lowliness of mind esteem others better than yourselves. Greatness in Jesus' kingdom stoops before it stands.
lens_gloss: greater — the comparing word the heart keeps asking, which Jesus answers by standing a child in the middle

note_body: Proverbs says the one who pities the poor is lending to the LORD Himself, and Jesus signs that ledger: ye did it unto me. Every unnoticed kindness has a royal recipient.
lens_gloss: without strength, weak, sick — the low estate in which the King chooses to be found and served

note_title: Job named the feet on the waves.
note_body: Job said God alone treadeth upon the waves of the sea — so the figure the disciples feared was wearing heaven's own signature. Fear called Him a ghost; Scripture had already called Him Lord.
lens_gloss: a phantom, an apparition — the name fear gives the Lord before faith has a chance to recognize Him

note_title: What the heart stores, the mouth spends.
note_body: The psalmist links them the same way Jesus does: the meditation of the heart becomes the speech of the mouth. Fill the storehouse with wisdom and the withdrawals take care of themselves.
lens_gloss: a storehouse, a treasury — what the heart lays up in secret and inevitably spends in speech and deed

note_title: Commandments with love as their sum.
note_body: Paul gathers the very commandments Jesus lists and names their total: love thy neighbour as thyself. The commands are not love's rival — they are love's clear practice.
lens_gloss: a commandment, a charge — love given clear edges so it can be practiced, not merely felt

note_body: The vine explains the counting-house: what bears fruit is tended toward more, and what refuses to grow is finally lost. Grace was never meant for storage — it multiplies only in motion.
lens_gloss: to overflow, to abound — the increase God adds to whatever received grace is put into motion

note_title: Isaiah warned us about the packaging.
note_body: Isaiah said the Servant would carry no form nor comeliness that we should desire Him, and Nazareth proved it — they saw a carpenter and stumbled over glory. God still hides majesty inside humble form.
lens_gloss: a builder, a craftsman in wood — the workman's title the hometown crowd used to shrink the Lord of glory

note_body: Israel was commanded to love the LORD with all the heart, and here Jesus quietly claims that very place — above father, mother, son, daughter. Only God may ask for the whole heart, and Jesus asks.
lens_gloss: warm, family-hearted affection — the dearest natural love, which Jesus asks to take second place to Him

note_body: Philadelphia hears I will keep thee, and Peter adds the credential: the Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly. Your endurance is not self-storage — it is guarded custody in experienced hands.
lens_gloss: to guard, to watch over and hold safe — kept obedience answered by keeping grace, the same word both directions

note_title: The warning that became church history.
note_body: What Jesus foretold in Matthew, Acts records plainly: Herod stretched forth his hands to vex the church. The disciples were not caught off guard — they walked into hostile rooms already prepared by their Lord's honesty.
lens_gloss: to pay close attention, to be on guard — clear-eyed preparation for pressure, not fearful retreat from it

note_title: Joseph's brothers and the vineyard tenants.
note_body: Joseph's brothers saw the beloved son coming and conspired to slay him — the same dark reasoning the tenants whisper over the heir. Grasping hearts repeat themselves, and in both stories God turns the plot into salvation.
lens_gloss: the heir, the one to whom everything rightfully belongs — the Son the tenants recognize and still refuse

note_title: Failure asked its question in private.
note_body: Mark remembers the same moment and adds where it happened — in the house, away from the crowd that had watched them fail. Jesus keeps a door open where public defeat can become private instruction.
lens_gloss: privately, on one's own — the shamed question finds Jesus away from the crowd, where honest weakness can be taught instead of judged.

note_body: The crowd's Hosanna is Psalm 118:25 set to footsteps — 'Save now, I beseech thee' turned into a song. The old plea for rescue rides into Jerusalem and is answered in Person.
lens_gloss: a Hebrew cry carried into Greek praise: 'save, please!' — the crowd sings a rescue plea to the very One able to answer it.

note_body: Proverbs promised that the wise would learn to understand a proverb and the dark sayings of the wise; in Matthew, Jesus sits His learners down and asks whether that old promise is coming true in them.
lens_gloss: to put together — understanding that gathers scattered pieces into one whole; Jesus checks whether His stories have assembled into living truth.

note_body: In Egypt even Pharaoh's magicians ran out of imitation and confessed, 'This is the finger of God.' Jesus takes up that very phrase to announce that the same delivering hand is now at work through Him.
lens_gloss: finger — the smallest measure of God's strength; one finger of His is more than enough to break what holds a life captive.

note_body: Proverbs names the trap — the fear of man — and Matthew shows Jesus refusing to step into it. He lets the offended walk away rather than trim the truth that saves.
lens_gloss: to spring the trap-stick, to take offense — truth can trip a proud heart; Jesus lets it, rather than soften what saves.

note_body: Isaiah had already described a Servant despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows. When Jesus says the Son of man must suffer, He is walking into a grief Scripture had long since made room for — with resurrection waiting on the far side.
lens_gloss: it is necessary — the small word of divine purpose; the suffering ahead is not fate closing in but the Father's plan unfolding.

note_body: 'What thinkest thou, Simon?' and 'Which now of these three, thinkest thou?' are the same Teacher at work. Jesus forms sons by drawing out their reasoning under His gaze, not by demanding compliance without understanding.
lens_gloss: to seem, to think — 'what seems right to you, Simon?' Jesus draws Peter's reasoning into the light before He shapes it.

note_body: Proverbs warns that whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will one day cry and not be heard. The forgiven servant lives out that proverb, jailing a debtor with hands mercy had just untied.
lens_gloss: to will, to be willing — the servant's cruelty was not lack of means but of willingness; mercy dies first in the will.

note_title: Still together in the upper room.
note_body: The unlikely names Mark lists show up again in Acts, still together in the upper room — Simon the zealot seated beside Matthew the tax man. What Jesus gathers, grace keeps holding together.
lens_gloss: from Aramaic qan'an, 'zealous one' — Simon the revolutionary, seated in the same Twelve as Matthew the tax man.

note_title: The light already dwells with Him.
note_body: Daniel blessed the God who reveals deep and secret things because the light dwells with Him. Luke 12:2 rests on that same fact: nothing stays covered, so the disciple need not fear what schemers hide.
lens_gloss: to unveil, uncover — every covering is temporary; God's daylight is already traveling toward each hidden thing, so fear loses its leverage.

note_title: The master wears the LORD's face.
note_body: Psalm 145 says the LORD is gracious, full of compassion, and great in mercy — and in the parable that very character stands up, cancels a hopeless debt, and sets a prisoner loose. Mercy is who God is before it is what He does.
lens_gloss: to be moved in the depths, gut-level compassion — mercy the master feels in his body before it opens his hands.

note_title: A table in the wilderness, again.
note_body: Israel once sneered, 'Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?' The disciples ask the same question in honest lack — and Jesus answers the old taunt with a meal and baskets left over.
lens_gloss: to feed until satisfied — the very word the disciples doubt is the word Mark uses moments later: 'they did eat, and were filled.'

note_body: The fast God chose in Isaiah — bread dealt to the hungry, the naked covered, our own flesh not hidden from — becomes the King's own checklist in Matthew 25. Mercy has always been how God's people are recognized.
lens_gloss: to look upon in order to care — the verb of God visiting His people, handed to disciples at sickbeds and prison doors.

note_title: Hold fast, because He is faithful.
note_body: Revelation says hold fast because He comes quickly; Hebrews says hold fast because He is faithful that promised. Same grip, same anchor — the utter trustworthiness of the returning Lord.
lens_gloss: to grip with strength — not anxious clutching but a deliberate, muscled hold on what Christ has already placed in your hands.

note_body: Ezekiel heard the Lord GOD promise to judge His own flock, between the rams and the goats. Matthew shows who holds that shepherd's office: the Son of man, sorting the nations with a shepherd's practiced eye.
lens_gloss: to mark off, set apart — a shepherd's practiced evening motion, finally sorting what grazed side by side all day long.

note_body: Moses begged the LORD to appoint a shepherd so the congregation would not be as sheep which have no shepherd, and God gave him Joshua. In Mark, Joshua's greater Namesake looks at shepherdless crowds and takes up the office Himself.
lens_gloss: shepherd — the presence that turns a scattered crowd back into a flock; Jesus sees the lack and answers it with Himself.

note_title: The ant and the buried talent.
note_body: Proverbs sends the hesitant to watch the ant, who works without excuse or overseer. In the parable the master uses that very word — slothful — for a servant whose fear had dressed itself up as prudence.
lens_gloss: shrinking, hesitant — the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for Proverbs' sluggard; sloth is fear that keeps postponing obedience.

note_body: What the servant only says in his heart — my lord delayeth — Peter hears spoken out loud by scoffers: 'Where is the promise of his coming?' Carelessness always begins as a quiet theory about God's slowness.
lens_gloss: to linger, take one's time — the heart's quiet theory about the Master's delay, granting itself permission to grow careless.

note_body: Proverbs promises that he who trusts in his riches shall fall, while the righteous flourish as a branch — rooted, not propped. Jesus speaks that same proverb at the very door of the kingdom, to astonished disciples.
lens_gloss: to be persuaded, to lean one's full weight — riches block the door only when a heart has settled its whole trust upon them.

note_title: Surprise is what blindness sounds like.
note_body: Malachi's priests asked 'Wherein have we despised thy name?' with the same honest surprise as the goats' 'When saw we thee?' Neglect rarely knows itself; it has to be shown the faces it walked past.
lens_gloss: to serve at table, to attend hands-on — what the surprised never did; they missed not a doctrine but a serving tray.

note_body: Matthew hears the father cry, 'Lord, have mercy on my son'; Luke leans in closer and hears why — 'he is mine only child.' Jesus receives family pain with all its particulars, not just its category.
lens_gloss: have mercy — the church's oldest cry, first learned by parents standing helpless beside children they love and cannot fix.

note_body: David sought out Mephibosheth to show him kindness 'for Jonathan's sake'; Jesus promises reward for water given 'because ye belong to Christ.' In both, the smallest mercy is measured by the name it honors.
lens_gloss: wages, reward — heaven keeps honest books; not one cup of cold water goes unrecorded in the King's ledger.

note_body: The Marcus greeting the churches from Peter's side is the same Mark Paul asks for by name at the end: 'he is profitable to me for the ministry.' In Christ's household, restored names get written back into the greetings.
lens_gloss: chosen-together — election is not a solitary certificate but a family membership; even in Babylon, nobody who belongs to Christ is chosen alone.

note_title: Touched, because He can be touched.
note_body: Hebrews says our High Priest is touched with the feeling of our infirmities; Matthew shows what that looks like from the roadside — fingers on blind eyes, then light, then a road walked together.
lens_gloss: to touch, take hold of — compassion that closes the distance and lays a hand exactly where the ache lives.

note_title: The King's beauty, promised and seen.
note_body: Isaiah promised, 'Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty.' On the high mountain three fishermen received that promise early, watching glory break through a face they thought they knew.
lens_gloss: to be transformed from within — glory not draped over Jesus but shining out of who He already was.

note_body: Ephesians says we were chosen in Him before the foundation of the world; Matthew's King hands over a kingdom prepared from that same beginning. The welcome is older than anything we could have done to earn it.
lens_gloss: to make ready beforehand — the kingdom was not assembled when you arrived; your welcome predates the world itself.

note_body: Mark keeps the companion saying that unlocks this one: the sabbath was made for man. The Lord of the Sabbath rules it as its Maker, so His authority always bends rest toward mercy, never mercy into burden.
lens_gloss: Lord, rightful owner — the Sabbath has a Master, and His name is mercy; rest is safest in the hands that made it.

note_body: Deuteronomy taught freed slaves to open their hands because 'thou wast a bondman... and the LORD thy God redeemed thee: therefore.' The master's rebuke runs on the same therefore — forgiven people are meant to become fluent in forgiving.
lens_gloss: to release, send away — a debt lifted off and carried out of sight, meant to teach the freed hands how to open.

note_title: The zealot who was set free.
note_body: The same tradition-keeping the Pharisees weaponize in Mark once ran hot in Paul's own veins, and he outdid his whole generation at it. It took meeting Jesus for him to learn that zeal for the elders' rules is not the same thing as love for God.
lens_gloss: a handing down; what is passed along — precious when it carries truth, dangerous the moment it starts measuring hearts.

note_title: Isaiah planted, Jesus finished the song.
note_body: Jesus' hearers knew Isaiah's old vineyard song, where the Owner Himself pulls down the hedge of an unfruitful field. When the Son retells it, the tenants learn what Judah learned: the vineyard was never theirs, and the Owner still comes looking for fruit in its season.
lens_gloss: the vineyard — God's cherished planting, let out to workers who tend it for the Owner's fruit, never for their own keeping.

note_body: Isaiah promised that those who wait on the LORD would one day watch their despisers bow, and would not be ashamed. In Revelation the risen Son takes that ancient promise into His own mouth and speaks it over one small, misjudged church He loves.
lens_gloss: to love with settled, choosing love — the vindication Jesus promises is less about enemies bowing than about you knowing 'I have loved thee.'

note_body: Moses commanded Israel not to hide from a brother's fallen animal but to help lift it up again. Jesus stands inside that same commandment and asks His critics why a hurting person on the sabbath deserves less than a sheep in a pit.
lens_gloss: to raise up — the very verb the Gospels use for resurrection; mercy is always reaching down into the pit to lift something out.

note_title: The Book that loves us straight.
note_body: Jesus traces error to its root: not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. Paul answers from the other side, that the God-breathed Book is given for reproof and correction — mercy in written form, meant to love our assumptions straight.
lens_gloss: to wander off the road, be led astray — error pictured not as stupidity but as drifting, and Scripture as the voice calling the wanderer home.

note_body: Elisha's servant protested, 'Should I set this before an hundred men?' — the same worry the disciples voice over five loaves. Both times the Lord simply says give, and the little that obeyed Him fed everyone with something left over.
lens_gloss: to give — Jesus' command 'give ye them' places the miracle's first motion into small, obedient, ordinary hands.

note_body: What Matthew introduces as a parable, Revelation announces as history: the marriage of the Lamb is come, and His bride has made herself ready. The King's invitation was never a cold summons — it was always headed toward that day of joy.
lens_gloss: a wedding feast — the kingdom pictured first not as a courtroom but as a celebration a Father prepares for His Son.

note_body: Centuries before this synagogue morning, Hosea carried God's heart to Israel: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice. Jesus' sabbath question simply holds that old desire up against their silence, and the silence tells on them.
lens_gloss: to save, rescue, make whole — Jesus' sabbath question in one word: does holy rest ever outrank the rescue of a life?

note_body: Jesus' sober word about receiving and losing finds its plain-spoken twin in Luke: unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required. Grace is a trust, and every truth He hands you is waiting on a living answer.
lens_gloss: to overflow, to abound — grace received and responded to does not merely hold steady; it multiplies past the brim.

note_title: Under the Teacher, becoming like Him.
note_body: Matthew sets the order: the student does not stand above the Master. Luke adds the promise hidden inside that order — stay teachable under Him long enough, and you will be shaped into His likeness.
lens_gloss: a learner — the disciple's very name is a posture: not one who has arrived, but one who stays under the Teacher's hand.

note_body: David cried that men compassed him with words of hatred and fought him without a cause, and that cry becomes the Son's own road out of that synagogue. A healed hand was the whole offense — and the mercy was still worth it.
lens_gloss: to destroy, to lose utterly — the verb they aimed at Jesus is the very ruin He had come to save them from.

note_title: He knows what is in us.
note_body: Luke says Jesus knew their thoughts; John says He never needed anyone to testify of man, for He knew what was in man. A divided heart is safe nowhere except laid open before the eyes that already see it and love it still.
lens_gloss: to be split into parts against itself — the quiet civil war Jesus names before it brings a kingdom or a heart to the ground.

note_body: Matthew gives us the mustard seed; Mark adds the heart — say to this mountain, and doubt not within. Faith's size matters far less than its aim, because the moving of mountains was always God's work, not ours.
lens_gloss: faith, trust — leaning your full weight on God; measured never by its own size but by the strength of the One it holds.

note_title: First and Last, in both Testaments.
note_body: Through Isaiah the LORD of hosts declares, I am the first, and I am the last; beside me there is no God. In Revelation the Son speaks that same name over His church — and every pressure that acts final has to answer to Him.
lens_gloss: the Almighty, the All-Ruler — the One whose grip holds every chapter, so no page of your story slips out of His hands.

note_body: The angels hastened Lot out of Sodom with his people and nothing else, because lingering meant being consumed. Jesus presses the same mercy-urgency on the housetop: when He says move, what is left in the house is not worth the soul.
lens_gloss: to pick up, carry off — the backward reach for baggage that can cost a runner everything when Christ is calling forward.

note_body: Matthew shows Jesus healing while He travels; Mark shows whole regions carrying their sick on beds to wherever they heard He was. With Jesus, the way itself becomes a place of healing — no errand is empty space to Him.
lens_gloss: to tend, care for, heal — bedside attention given on the open road, as if there were nowhere better to be.

note_body: The parable's severe ending and James' plain sentence say one thing: judgment is without mercy to the one who showed none. But James does not stop there — mercy, wherever it is finally given, still rejoices against judgment.
lens_gloss: the jailer, the tormentor — unforgiveness pictured as a debtor's prison the hard heart builds and then lives in.

note_body: The questioners reach back to Moses' provision in Deuteronomy, a concession written for hard times and hard hearts. Jesus lets them read it, then points past the paperwork to the healing God intended from the beginning.
lens_gloss: to permit, to allow — a concession made to hardened hearts; permission was never the same thing as God's healing intention.

note_body: Isaiah heard it first: in returning and rest shall ye be saved — and ye would not. The wedding guests echo that old refusal almost word for word, while the King's invitation stays as generous as ever.
lens_gloss: to will, to want — the feast fell empty not for lack of room but for lack of wanting; the King's table waits on the will.

note_title: The Master's eyes find the faithful.
note_body: The psalmist says God's eyes rest on the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with Him. Jesus blesses the servant found simply doing what was entrusted — heaven has always noticed hidden diligence.
lens_gloss: blessed, deeply happy — the quiet joy of a servant caught in the act of ordinary faithfulness when the Master comes.

note_body: Mark and Matthew describe the same lifted eyes and the same finding: no man any more, save Jesus only. The glory settles, the voices fade, and the center of everything is still standing there.
lens_gloss: alone, only — when the cloud lifts, the whole scene resolves to one figure; 'Jesus only' is the disciple's truest focus.

note_title: The touch that raises the fallen.
note_body: Daniel lay drained before the glory until one like the appearance of a man touched him and strengthened him. On the mountain the disciples fall the same way — and this time it is the Son's own hand that does the strengthening.
lens_gloss: to touch, take hold of — the Gospels' word for Jesus' healing contact; glory bends down and steadies trembling shoulders.

note_body: Ezekiel indicts shepherds who ruled the flock with force and cruelty instead of binding up the broken. Peter — the man Jesus told to feed His sheep — hands down the remedy: no lording over the heritage, only living examples the flock can trace.
lens_gloss: a pattern, an imprint struck like a stamp — leaders called to be living patterns the flock can safely trace their steps by.

note_title: No price in, no price out.
note_body: Isaiah's market call cries buy wine and milk without money and without price. Jesus sends His disciples out on that same economy: what came to you as a gift can only honestly leave your hands as one.
lens_gloss: freely, as a gift, without payment — grace carries no invoice, neither when it arrives nor when it is passed along.

note_title: The Owner asks for a verdict.
note_body: In Isaiah the LORD invites Jerusalem to judge between Him and His vineyard; in Mark, Jesus raises the same court question about the tenants and then answers it Himself. Either way the verdict lands — and every honest steward feels their own case being read.
lens_gloss: lord, owner, master — the vineyard was never tenant property; the parable's whole question is whose it always was.

note_title: Isaiah's sign on the Jericho road.
note_body: Isaiah promised the day when the eyes of the blind would be opened. Two roadside voices call out to the Son of David for mercy, and the ancient promise stops walking and stands still for them.
lens_gloss: to have mercy — the beggar's cry, need dropping its manners and calling out loud because the Lord is passing near.

note_body: Ezekiel saw water flowing from the sanctuary, trees bearing fruit every month, leaves for medicine. John watches that same river arrive in the New Jerusalem, where at last the leaves are for the healing of the nations.
lens_gloss: healing, tending care — the Bible's last chapter gives the nations not a verdict but a cure.

note_body: Matthew hears sword, Luke hears fire — two figures for the same holy disturbance. When the Son arrives, quiet arrangements built on avoidance cannot keep pretending to be peace, and what He unsettles He unsettles to heal.
lens_gloss: the short sword — truth's cutting edge that divides false peace from real, not to wound but to make things honest.

note_title: An old promise finds its lungs.
note_body: Jeremiah said the wholehearted seeker would find God, and Bartimaeus proves it with his whole voice — the crowd's hush cannot outlast a heart that wants mercy that badly.
lens_gloss: a raw, unpolished shout — the cry of a man who would rather be loud than unhealed.

note_body: Israel once sneered, "Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?" On this desert evening Jesus answers the old doubt with bread enough and baskets left over.
lens_gloss: a desolate, empty place — precisely the setting where God has always loved to set a table.

note_body: Jesus speaks the hard word on the mission road, and Paul sets it into an early church song from prison — allegiance to the Son was never meant to be a private opinion.
lens_gloss: to disown, to say "I do not know him" — allegiance broken out loud, the wound Jesus takes seriously.

note_title: Two Gospels keep the small slip.
note_body: Mark and Matthew both write down the forgotten loaves, and in both accounts Jesus uses the empty basket to teach rather than to shame — He is patient with our practical lapses.
lens_gloss: to let something slip the mind — ordinary human forgetting, which Jesus meets with instruction instead of scorn.

note_title: The feast door and the city gate.
note_body: The man without a garment cannot stay at the feast, and Revelation shows the same holy line at the city gate — only what the Lamb has covered comes in, so grace must be worn, not merely admired.
lens_gloss: darkness — the far outside where the feast's light no longer reaches; the opposite of the covered place at the table.

note_body: David says God put a new song in his rescued mouth, and heaven's redeemed sing one too — redemption always teaches the tongue fresh language to answer the old sentences pain repeats.
lens_gloss: to purchase in the marketplace — the Lamb paid in His own blood to buy people back for God.

note_title: Daniel saw the same two roads.
note_body: Centuries earlier Daniel watched the sleepers wake to two destinies, and Jesus stands at the close of that vision to tell us plainly that the dividing line runs through mercy lived or withheld.
lens_gloss: belonging to the age to come — the same weighty word measures both destinies, which is why Jesus speaks with such care.

note_body: Mark says they were amazed as Jesus strode ahead toward His suffering, and Isaiah had already said many would be astonished at the Servant — the Jerusalem road walks straight into that old prophecy.
lens_gloss: to be gripped with awe — the stunned amazement of watching Jesus walk first into what everyone else flees.

note_body: God told Noah plainly what was coming, so the ones swept away were not uninformed but unlistening — Jesus wakes us now so His coming finds us watching, not lulled.
lens_gloss: to know by noticing — the tragedy of the flood generation was not missing information but refusing to perceive.

note_title: Even the donkeys were accounted for.
note_body: Samuel sent Saul down a road where every small detail was already arranged, and Jesus does the same with a tied colt — the King's foreknowledge reaches into ropes and doorways, so simple obedience walks on prepared ground.
lens_gloss: to find exactly as promised — obedience discovers what the Lord has already gone ahead and arranged.

note_title: Rules saw the bed, not the man.
note_body: In Mark hungry disciples are accused, and in John a man carrying his sickbed after thirty-eight years hears only "not lawful" — both scenes show how fast religion can inspect while mercy is still rejoicing.
lens_gloss: what is permitted — the measuring word of the accusers, which Jesus answers with mercy's deeper law.

note_title: Five centuries between promise and hoofbeats.
note_body: Zechariah told Zion her King would come lowly, riding a colt, and Matthew watches it happen in the street — gentleness was not a change of plan; it was the plan all along.
lens_gloss: meek — strength under gentle rein; power that refuses to crush the very people it comes to save.

note_body: Ruth asked why grace would notice a foreigner, and Boaz's kindness folded her into David's own family line — centuries later a Canaanite mother calls on that family name, Son of David, and finds the same wide welcome.
lens_gloss: to show active mercy — not pity felt at a distance but compassion that moves, the cry Jesus never finally refuses.

note_title: He said it twice, on purpose.
note_body: Jesus gives this same hard warning when He first sends the Twelve and again on the Mount of Olives — He repeats what wounds most because He would rather prepare His own than protect them with silence.
lens_gloss: to hand over, to betray — the very word used of Jesus' own betrayal; He knows this wound from the inside.

note_title: David praised his fear down to size.
note_body: Jesus calls His friends away from fearing those who can only touch the body, and David shows how it is done — praising God's word until flesh and its threats shrink to their true measure.
lens_gloss: friend — Jesus steadies fearful hearts by naming them His own before He ever names the danger.

note_title: Peter and Paul tell one story.
note_body: Neither the fisherman nor the Pharisee reasoned his way to Christ — Peter heard from the Father, Paul says the Son was revealed in him, and both confess that flesh and blood had no part in it.
lens_gloss: to unveil what was hidden — knowing who Jesus is comes as the Father's gift, not the mind's achievement.

note_body: The tree of life stood in Eden's midst before shame ever entered the story, and Scripture's last page shows blessed ones walking through gates to reach it — Jesus turns humanity's oldest exile into homecoming.
lens_gloss: blessed, deeply well — the Bible's final beatitude, spoken over those who come home through the gates.

note_title: Job said only God walks there.
note_body: Job named it as God's own signature — treading upon the waves of the sea — so when Jesus comes striding across the storm in the dark watch, He is signing His name where only God can walk.
lens_gloss: to walk about — the ordinary word for walking, here done on storm water, as though the sea were a road.

note_title: From village roads to Caesar's doorstep.
note_body: Jesus sends the Twelve out saying the kingdom is near, and Acts closes with that same kingdom still being preached in Rome, no man forbidding — the message He set walking has never stopped traveling.
lens_gloss: to draw near — the kingdom is not distant news to wait for but a nearness already arriving.

note_body: Jesus is quoting the words God gave Isaiah at his calling — fat heart, heavy ears, shut eyes — yet both passages end at the same open door: conversion and healing are still what He wants.
lens_gloss: to heal — the final word of the hard saying; underneath the warning, healing is still Jesus' desire.

note_body: Moses told Israel God would raise up a Prophet — "unto him ye shall hearken" — and on the mountain, with Moses himself standing by, the Father speaks the fulfillment: this is my beloved Son; hear Him.
lens_gloss: to hear with heed — the Father's entire command on the mountain gathers into one listening word.

note_title: The debt's size, the love's size.
note_body: The servant's plea from the floor uncovers a debt no man could pay, and in Simon's house Jesus adds the other half — the one forgiven most loves most, so mercy seen at full size becomes love at full strength.
lens_gloss: to be long-tempered, patient — the servant begs for the very patience God's mercy has already stretched wide.

note_title: A vine question only grace answers.
note_body: Through Jeremiah, God asks how His noble vine turned degenerate, and Jesus answers at the root — He does not paint good fruit onto bad branches; He makes the tree good.
lens_gloss: fruit — the visible yield that tells the honest truth about the hidden root.

note_title: Mark names the sons; Matthew, the mother.
note_body: Set side by side, the two Gospels show a whole family reaching for seats of honor, and Jesus receives them without scorn — untangling love from ambition with a question about a cup.
lens_gloss: to want, to will — Jesus does not crush desire; He converts it, teaching the heart what to want.

note_title: The promised light takes a seat.
note_body: Isaiah said the gloom by the way of the sea in Galilee would not last, and Matthew shows Jesus seated on a Galilean mountainside — the promised light does not arrive frantic; it sits down among the people and stays.
lens_gloss: to sit, to be settled — the unhurried posture of a teacher fully present and available.

note_title: Guests who never sent an inquiry.
note_body: The king's servants gather people who had no invitation in hand, and Paul names the wonder out loud — God lets Himself be found by those who never went looking, because grace travels to the road first.
lens_gloss: to call, to invite — the gospel's verb: a summons that turns strangers on a road into wedding guests.

note_title: Daniel's vision steps into the lampstands.
note_body: Daniel saw one like the Son of man approaching the Ancient of Days in glory, and John sees that same figure not far off in the clouds but standing among the churches — the glorious One keeps company with His people.
lens_gloss: in the midst — not above His people or beyond them, but standing right among them.

note_title: A psalmist's schedule, a Savior's mountain.
note_body: David kept evening, morning, and noon as appointments God would surely hear, and Jesus dismisses a whole crowd to keep His own appointment on the mountain — prayer that is protected, never leftover.
lens_gloss: to pray — the Son's own steady habit of turning from the crowd to the Father's face.

note_body: Jesus tells His disciples not to collect the title Rabbi, and James — writing to 'my brethren' — refuses to let the church become a room full of masters. Both passages guard the same treasure: one Teacher, and a family of learners at His feet.
lens_gloss: brothers — literally 'from one womb'; kinship that levels every title, because all of us learned at the same Teacher's feet.

note_title: The psalm Jesus carried into the temple.
note_body: Centuries before the tables turned over, David sang of a zeal for God's house that consumes a man whole. When Jesus drives out the sellers, that old song stands up and walks through the courts.
lens_gloss: to drive out, cast out — the very verb used when Jesus expels unclean spirits; He clears the house so prayer can live there.

note_body: David cries, 'Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul,' and Peter compresses that same psalm into three wet words. The prayer that reached heaven from the deep now reaches a hand across the waves.
lens_gloss: to rescue, deliver, make whole — Peter's whole theology shrank to one word, and one word was enough to reach the Savior's hand.

note_body: Proverbs says guard the heart, for out of it are the issues of life; Jesus follows that stream all the way to the mouth. Keep the spring, and the water that spills into your words will run clean.
lens_gloss: a storehouse, treasury — the heart as a vault; whatever gets deposited there is the currency the mouth will one day spend.

note_body: Isaiah says all flesh is grass and its goodliness a fading flower; the fig tree's overnight withering shows the same truth up close. What only looks alive cannot survive the Lord's inspection — but what He plants endures.
lens_gloss: to dry up, wither — sudden dryness exposing that no hidden life was ever feeding the leaves everyone admired from a distance.

note_title: Saints have always asked how long.
note_body: By the river in Daniel's vision, one asks the man clothed in linen, 'How long shall it be to the end of these wonders?' — the very question the disciples carry to Jesus on the mount. God has never shamed His people for asking; He draws the questioner closer.
lens_gloss: a sign, a marker pointing beyond itself — the disciples ask for one, and Jesus answers by teaching them to watch with Him.

note_body: Zechariah stood before a vision he could not read and simply asked the one beside him. The disciples do the same once the crowd goes home — and in both houses, humility is what receives the interpretation.
lens_gloss: a placing alongside — a story laid next to life; its depths open not to the crowd but to those who come and ask.

note_body: In the upper room Jesus says plainly, 'I have overcome the world,' and in Revelation the risen Lord offers His own throne to those who overcome as He did. The seat is promised, and the path to it has already been walked.
lens_gloss: to conquer, prevail — the victory Christ has already won and now shares with everyone who stays faithful through the struggle.

note_title: A hole in the ground, a napkin.
note_body: One servant buries his lord's money in the earth; another wraps his pound in a napkin — fear always finds a wrapping. Both parables warn that playing it safe with God's gift is not safety at all.
lens_gloss: to hide, conceal — the verb of buried treasure and buried fear; what fear hides away, grace calls back into daylight and use.

note_title: The mountain's secret and the empty tomb.
note_body: 'Tell no man till the Son of man be risen' — and on resurrection morning the messengers at the empty tomb say, 'Remember how he spake unto you.' The silence Jesus asked for had a release date, and Easter is when the sealed testimony opens.
lens_gloss: to stand up, rise — the mountain's secret waited on this verb; resurrection is the appointed hour that unseals testimony.

note_title: A trap question, a redemption story.
note_body: The Sadducees hold up the brother's-duty law as a puzzle; Ruth shows the same law carried out in love, raising up the name of the dead. What they used to test Jesus, God had already used to bring Him — through Boaz's line to Bethlehem.
lens_gloss: to raise up — the resurrection root standing quietly inside the very law the Sadducees quoted to argue resurrection away.

note_body: When leaders demanded silence at the triumphal entry, Jesus answered that the very stones would cry out; in the temple He receives the children's Hosanna over priestly displeasure. Praise for the Son of David will find a voice — the only question is whether ours joins it.
lens_gloss: from Hebrew hoshia-na, 'save, we pray' — a cry for rescue turned into praise, sounding truest on the children's lips.

note_title: Two by two was always wisdom.
note_body: The Preacher says two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labour; Jesus builds that old wisdom into the first sending. Nobody walks the mission road alone — nearness to Him comes with a companion for the way.
lens_gloss: to call to oneself — mission begins as a summons into nearness; Jesus draws the Twelve close before He ever sends them out.

note_body: Elisha's own servant ran after silver and turned grace into a transaction; centuries later another trusted man, close to a greater Master, does the same. Jesus names Judas among the twelve without flinching — He has always known what nearness alone cannot guarantee.
lens_gloss: to hand over, deliver up — Judas' verb, yet Scripture says Jesus 'was delivered for our offences'; God's purpose ran deeper than treachery.

note_body: Moses told Israel that God would raise up a Prophet from among their brethren — 'unto him ye shall hearken.' The crowd's answer names the Prophet correctly; obedience is what finishes the sentence.
lens_gloss: one who speaks forth for God — the crowd's title was true but unfinished; Moses said of the promised Prophet, 'unto him hearken.'

note_body: Jesus says cut off what drags you toward destruction; Paul translates the surgery into daily discipleship — 'mortify therefore your members.' The knife is not cruelty; it is love refusing to negotiate with what kills.
lens_gloss: to trip up, ensnare — from skandalon, the bait-stick of a trap; Jesus names whatever keeps baiting the soul toward ruin.

note_body: At the end of his life David testified, 'The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue.' Jesus promises His disciples the same supply: when the moment outsizes you, the Father's Spirit does the speaking.
lens_gloss: breath, wind, spirit — the Father's own breath supplying words at the exact moment yours run out.

note_title: She left everything and found harvest.
note_body: Boaz names Ruth's cost out loud — father, mother, homeland, all left behind — and God answers it with a field of grace, a redeemer, and a place in Messiah's own line. What obedience releases, the kingdom multiplies.
lens_gloss: to release, let go — the same verb Scripture uses for forgiving debts; what a disciple releases, God never lets fall to waste.

note_body: James points to Rahab the harlot, justified when her faith became action; Jesus says the harlots enter the kingdom ahead of the polished answerers. Heaven reads obedience, not old labels.
lens_gloss: to go before, lead the way — the despised are not merely admitted; they walk in front, showing the proud what surrender looks like.

note_title: Count the loaves, pour the oil.
note_body: Elisha began with the widow's honest little — one pot of oil — poured out behind a shut door until every vessel was full; Jesus begins with an honest count of seven loaves. God's multiplication has always started with an unexaggerated inventory placed in His hands.
lens_gloss: a loaf of bread — ordinary daily provision; Jesus counts what is actually in your hands before He multiplies it.

note_body: The list that begins with 'Simon, who is called Peter' ends on the foundations of the New Jerusalem, where the names of the twelve apostles are written into the city's wall. When Jesus names you for following, He is writing something eternity keeps.
lens_gloss: a name — identity known and spoken; the names Jesus calls on a Galilean road are the ones eternity carves in stone.

note_title: An old promise, the last invitation.
note_body: Isaiah heard God promise water on the thirsty and His Spirit poured on dry ground; Revelation's closing page opens the tap — the Spirit and the bride say, Come. The Bible's last invitation is the prophet's promise finally flowing free.
lens_gloss: freely, as a gift, without payment — the same word Paul uses for justification; heaven's last page repeats heaven's price: none.

note_title: The crowd asked; the gospel answers.
note_body: 'Is not this the son of David?' the amazed people wonder — and Paul opens Romans with the settled confession: Jesus Christ our Lord, made of the seed of David according to the flesh. A holy question, held near long enough, becomes a creed.
lens_gloss: to be beside oneself with astonishment — wonder that unsettles old certainties and makes room for a brand-new confession.

note_title: He came looking for fruit before.
note_body: Isaiah sang of a vineyard given every advantage that yielded only wild grapes; Jesus walks to a leafy fig tree and finds nothing but foliage. The Owner has always drawn near expecting fruit — and nearness is where profession gets tested.
lens_gloss: leaves — the foliage of profession, green and promising from far away; only nearness can test the branches for fruit.

note_title: Rooted by the river, or scorched.
note_body: The psalm's tree planted by rivers of water has leaves that never wither; the seedling in Jesus' parable dies in one hot afternoon for want of root. The difference is not the sun — both trees felt it — but the hidden water underneath.
lens_gloss: root — the unseen lifeline below the surface; what keeps a plant alive in the heat never shows above the ground.

note_body: Before the flood interrupted the eating and the marrying, God's word to Noah was an invitation: 'Come thou and all thy house.' Jesus recalls those days so His people will hear the same mercy in time — awake, and safely inside.
lens_gloss: day — plain, repeated, ordinary time; the days of Noah remind us that watchfulness is decided in the unremarkable hours.

note_title: Signs were never the whole test.
note_body: Moses warned that a prophet might produce a real wonder and still be leading Israel away from the LORD; Jesus repeats the warning for the last days. God's people were never meant to follow fireworks — only the voice they already know.
lens_gloss: a false anointed one — a counterfeit close enough to demand discernment; only nearness to the true Christ exposes the imitation.

note_title: The stranger at the door is more.
note_body: Hebrews says some who welcomed strangers entertained angels unawares; Jesus goes further — the neglected stranger was Himself. Either way, we never know less than heaven when we open the door.
lens_gloss: stranger, foreigner, guest — the unrecognized one at the door in whom Christ Himself waits to be received.

note_title: A field, a lion, one watchword.
note_body: Jesus tells of an enemy sowing while men slept; Peter gives the saints their posture toward that enemy — sober and vigilant, watchful but never frantic. The field still belongs to the Master, so we watch with steady eyes, not shaking hands.
lens_gloss: darnel, a weed that mimics wheat until harvest — the Teacher's word for evil that patience, not panic, will finally sort out.

note_body: The rich ruler tossed "good" around like a compliment; the psalmist had already learned where goodness lives — Thou art good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes. Right obedience starts by looking at the good God, not at our own reflection.
lens_gloss: good in essence, not in performance — a goodness that belongs first to God and reaches us only as grace.

note_body: Old Lamech boasted that his revenge would run seventy-and-sevenfold; Jesus takes up the very same number and turns it inside out. Where sin multiplied vengeance, the Kingdom multiplies mercy.
lens_gloss: seventy times — a number built to break the counting habit, carrying mercy past the last edge of arithmetic.

note_body: The lawyer's answer is Israel's oldest daily prayer, straight from Moses — love the Lord with all thine heart, soul, and might. Jesus receives the Shema and turns it into a road to walk with Him.
lens_gloss: to love with full-hearted allegiance — devotion of the whole self, willed and walked out, not a passing feeling.

note_body: The vineyard master and the waiting father speak the same gentle correction: son, all that I have is thine. Grace given to another never subtracts one thing from you.
lens_gloss: I will, I choose — the master's generosity is deliberate delight, never an oversight to be corrected by our comparing.

note_title: Abram's road runs through the Gospel.
note_body: Before Jesus ever named the cost of following, God called Abram out of country, kindred, and his father's house — with a promise waiting on the other side. Every leaving for Jesus' sake walks that old road, and it has always led to blessing.
lens_gloss: to release, to let go — the same verb Scripture uses for forgiving; leaving for Jesus' sake is an open hand, not a torn one.

note_title: The waiting ones get their gladness.
note_body: Isaiah pictures a people who waited and then rejoice — lo, this is our God; we have waited for him. Jesus sets that same gladness at midnight: readiness is not dread, it is a lamp trimmed for a wedding.
lens_gloss: bridegroom — the long-awaited divine husband arriving in person; the midnight cry ends in a wedding, not a verdict.

note_body: What Jesus promised the woman at the well — water springing up into everlasting life — John finally sees full-grown: a crystal river running from the throne of God and of the Lamb. The well inside becomes the river at the end.
lens_gloss: God's own kind of life — not mere survival but unending vitality, flowing clear from the throne to thirsty people.

note_title: The furnace knew this paradox first.
note_body: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego opened their hands on their own lives before the furnace door ever opened — but if not, we will not bow. They lived the paradox before Jesus preached it: life released to God is life found.
lens_gloss: the soul-life, the self we clutch — lost when grasped, found and kept when placed in the hands of Christ.

note_title: Near the Teacher, far in heart.
note_body: Ezekiel watched people sit close, listen sweetly, and walk out with hearts chasing gain; Mark shows the same sorrowful step away from Jesus. Nearness to the Teacher is not yet surrender to Him.
lens_gloss: possessions, acquired holdings — the things a man owns that, left unwatched, quietly begin to own the man.

note_body: Matthew says salute the house; Luke opens the same instruction and shows what is folded inside it — first say, Peace be to this house. The disciple's opening word is a gift laid down at the door.
lens_gloss: to greet warmly, to embrace with words — a blessing set down at the door before any proof is offered.

note_body: Jesus says the surrendered life is the saved one, and Paul hands Timothy the church's settled echo — if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him. Losing for Christ's sake was never really loss.
lens_gloss: to save, rescue, make whole — the saving self-protection cannot manage, and surrendered trust receives from Jesus.

note_title: The psalmist promised this right hand.
note_body: David sang that in the midst of trouble God would stretch forth His hand and save; on the sea that promise closes around Peter's wrist. Jesus is the saving right hand in person.
lens_gloss: little-faith — Jesus' tender nickname for a held disciple; the correction comes after the rescue, spoken inside His grip.

note_body: Jesus commands readiness for an hour no one can predict; John shows what the ready ones are actually dressed for — the marriage of the Lamb. Preparation is not fear of loss but love expecting its feast.
lens_gloss: ready, prepared beforehand — a lamp already trimmed, a heart kept in position, so the sudden hour finds nothing in a panic.

note_title: Heaven's decree, spoken in a boat.
note_body: Psalm 2 carries the Father's decree — Thou art my Son; drenched disciples in a quieted boat arrive at the same words from the other side of a storm. Worship is the only fitting reply.
lens_gloss: to bow low in homage — the body's honest answer once the storm reveals who has been in the boat.

note_body: Caleb followed the Lord fully while a whole camp shrank back, because another spirit was in him. Jesus names how such following happens: the self denied, the cross taken up, the feet turned after Him.
lens_gloss: to deny utterly, to disown — the self stepped down from its throne so the followed One can truly lead.

note_body: Long before, God sent Elijah into Sidon's country where a widow was already appointed to meet him; when Jesus walks those same coasts, mercy is again out ahead of Him. Unfamiliar ground is still assigned ground.
lens_gloss: to withdraw, to move off to another region — Jesus' deliberate steps carrying mercy beyond the familiar map.

note_body: David marveled that anything offered to God was God's own already — of thine own have we given thee. The righteous in Jesus' parable share that astonishment: mercy done so freely it never counted itself.
lens_gloss: righteous, set right with God — a rightness so woven into the life that it forgets to keep receipts.

note_body: Jesus points His accusers back to the day David asked the priest for loaves in his need. The Son of David reads that story the way heaven wrote it — need met by mercy is Scripture kept, not broken.
lens_gloss: need, real human necessity — the lack Jesus reads with mercy while rule-keepers read it with suspicion.

note_body: Psalm 110 waited a thousand years for its full weight; Jesus opens it and shows Messiah already seated at the right hand. Every unfinished enemy sits on His schedule, not ours.
lens_gloss: Lord, rightful master — David's own descendant seated at God's right hand, holding authority no earthly throne conferred.

note_body: Peter reaches for tent poles; Paul says the same glory arrives another way — God shines it into hearts, in the face of Jesus Christ. Holy moments are received, not built.
lens_gloss: a tent, a booth — Peter's offer to house a glory that had already chosen its dwelling in Christ Himself.

note_title: Root and offspring, both at once.
